case_studies.title: Position: A Three-Layer Probabilistic Assume-Guarantee Architecture Is Structurally Required for Safe LLM Agent Deployment
case_studies.abstract: This position paper argues that enforcing LLM agent safety within a single abstraction layer is not merely suboptimal but categorically insufficient for deployed LLM agents -- a structural consequence of how agent execution works, not a contingent limitation of current systems. The three dimensions that jointly constitute safe operation -- semantic intent and policy compliance, environmental validity, and dynamical feasibility -- each depend on a strictly distinct set of information that becomes available at different stages of execution. No single guardrail can certify all three. We argue tha
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring safe deployment of Large Language Model (LLM) agents by proposing a three-layer probabilistic architecture. The authors argue that a single layer is not enough to guarantee safety, and their proposed architecture addresses this issue. The result is a safer and more reliable way to deploy LLM agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM agent deployments, here is what to do: assess your current safety guardrails, consider implementing a three-layer probabilistic architecture to address semantic intent, environmental validity, and dynamical feasibility. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM agents, check your current safety measures to ensure they are sufficient. Review your deployment protocols to ensure they align with the proposed architecture.

Novelty: The paper proposes a three-layer probabilistic assume-guarantee architecture for safe LLM agent deployment, which is relevant to AI researchers but might be surprising for IT engineers.
IT Relevance: This directly affects how IT engineers work on deploying large language models, but as a position paper, it doesn't provide actionable solutions. 
Value 90 Days: The architecture has potential for real-world applications, but the paper does not provide enough information for IT engineers to implement it within 90 days.

case_studies.title: EXG: Self-Evolving Agents with Experience Graphs
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex reasoning and problem solving through multi-step interactions, yet most deployed agents remain behaviorally static, with knowledge acquired during execution rarely translating into systematic improvement over time. In response, a growing line of work on self-evolving agents explores how agents can improve through experience during deployment, but most existing approaches either rely on ad hoc reflection limited to single-task correction or adopt unstructured memory that accumulates fragmented experience wi
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language model-based agents being behaviorally static by introducing self-evolving agents that improve over time through experience graphs. The researchers built a system that enables agents to systematically learn from experience and adapt to new situations. The result is a more dynamic and effective agent that can improve its performance over time.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on artificial intelligence and machine learning agent development, but IT managers responsible for AI or ML systems may want to monitor this technology for potential future applications.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: Introduces self-evolving agents, which is a novel aspect for some in IT. Relevance: Directly affects how IT engineers work with LLM APIs and agent systems. Value: Could be used to automate improvement of deployed agents, but implementation details are unclear. Overall score is around 49.

case_studies.title: SkillGenBench: Benchmarking Skill Generation Pipelines for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly built around reusable skills, a central challenge is no longer only whether agents can use provided skills, but whether they can generate correct, reusable, and executable skills from repositories and documents. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate the efficacy of given skills or the ability of agents to solve downstream tasks from raw context, but they do not isolate skill generation itself as the object of study. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating how well large language models can generate skills from existing information, the researchers built a benchmark called SkillGenBench to test this, and the result is a unified way to evaluate skill generation pipelines. The benchmark allows for comparing different skill generation methods. This is mainly relevant to AI and machine learning development.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on AI model development and evaluation, but it may be of interest to IT teams involved in AI or machine learning projects.

The tool could theoretically be used to evaluate and improve LLM skills generation pipelines, but the connection to real-world IT infrastructure is weak.

case_studies.summary: The ADR system solves the problem of securing AI agents in enterprise settings by addressing limited observability and insufficient robustness. The researchers built a large-scale framework for detecting and responding to AI security threats. The result is a production-proven system that improves the security of AI agents operating through the Model Context Protocol.

case_studies.title: Remembering More, Risking More: Longitudinal Safety Risks in Memory-Equipped LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Safety evaluations of memory-equipped LLM agents typically measure within-task safety: whether an agent completes a single scenario safely, often under adversarial conditions such as prompt injection or memory poisoning. In deployment, however, a single agent serves many independent tasks over a long horizon, and memory accumulated during earlier tasks can affect behavior on later, unrelated ones. Studying this regime requires evaluation along the temporal dimension across tasks: not whether an agent is safe at any single memory state, but how its safety profile changes as memory accumulates a
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of long-term safety risks in memory-equipped large language model (LLM) agents, where the accumulation of memory can affect behavior on later tasks. The authors built a framework to evaluate the safety of these agents over time, studying how their safety profile changes as memory accumulates. The result highlights potential safety risks in deploying memory-equipped LLM agents in real-world applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses LLM agents, here is what to do: review your agent's memory accumulation and retention policies, check for potential safety risks in multi-task scenarios, and consider implementing additional safety measures to mitigate these risks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses a specific aspect of safety in memory-equipped LLM agents, which is relevant to developers and engineers working with such systems. While the topic is novel, it may not directly impact IT engineers' work without further research. The value within 90 days is limited, but IT professionals with an interest in LLMs and safety might be interested in exploring this.

case_studies.title: GIM: Evaluating models via tasks that integrate multiple cognitive domains
case_studies.abstract: As LLM benchmarks saturate, the evaluation community has pursued two strategies to increase difficulty: escalating knowledge demands (GPQA, HLE) or removing knowledge entirely in favor of abstract reasoning (ARC-AGI). The first conflates memorization with capability; the second divorces reasoning from the practical contexts in which it matters. We take a different approach. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating large language models' abilities by creating a benchmark that tests their integration of multiple cognitive domains. The researchers built the Grounded Integration Measure, a benchmark of 820 original problems. The result provides a new way to evaluate language models' capabilities beyond memorization and abstract reasoning.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating large language models' abilities rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel approach to LLM benchmarking, but its relevance to IT engineering is limited. While it discusses the evaluation of LLMs, it does not reveal surprising insights about IT tools or systems. An IT engineer may forward the paper to a colleague as a theoretical concept, but it lacks practical applications.

case_studies.title: Advancing Narrative Long Video Generation via Training-Free Identity-Aware Memory
case_studies.abstract: Autoregressive video generation has improved rapidly in visual fidelity and interactivity, but it still suffers from long-term inconsistency and memory degradation. Most existing solutions either compress historical frames using predefined strategies or retrieve keyframes based on coarse implicit attention signals, both of which fail to handle evolving prompts with shifting entity references, leading to identity drift, character duplication, and attribute loss. To address this, we propose IAMFlow, a training-free identity-aware memory framework that explicitly models and tracks persistent enti
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of long-term inconsistency and memory degradation in video generation by building a training-free identity-aware memory framework called IAMFlow, which resulted in improved handling of evolving prompts with shifting entity references. The framework explicitly models and tracks persistent entities in videos. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: LivePI: More Realistic Benchmarking of Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injectio
case_studies.abstract: AI agents such as OpenClaw are increasingly deployed in local workflows with access to external tools. This creates indirect prompt-injection (IPI) risk: an agent may execute harmful instructions embedded in untrusted inputs such as email, downloaded files, webpages, repositories, or group-chat messages. Existing evaluations are often small, purely simulated, or focused on a narrow set of channels. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of indirect prompt injection risk in AI agents by creating a benchmark called LivePI to test the vulnerability of agents in a production-like environment, the result is a more realistic evaluation of IPI risk, which affects the security of local workflows. The researchers built LivePI to cover seven input surfaces and twelve attack/rendering families. This research is relevant to IT work as it highlights the importance of testing AI agents against IPI risk.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered systems with access to external tools, here is what to do: step 1, assess your current vulnerability to indirect prompt injection risk, step 2, consider using LivePI benchmark to test your systems, step 3, implement additional security measures to mitigate IPI risk.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While IT relevance is high due to the focus on IPI risk and agent interactions, novelty and value 90 days are impacted by the purely academic nature of the research and the simulated environment. The potential impact is mostly theoretical at this point. However, IT engineers would be interested in this work as it touches on their real-world concerns with agent deployments and potential security risks.

case_studies.title: Episodic-Semantic Memory Architecture for Long-Horizon Scientific Agents
case_studies.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into persistent scientific collaborators, context window saturation has emerged as a critical bottleneck. Scientific workflows involving iterative data analysis and hypothesis refinement rapidly saturate even extended contexts with dense technical content, while monolithic approaches suffer from quadratic cost scaling and cognitive degradation. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of context window saturation in Large Language Models, building a Dual Process Memory Architecture that separates short-term and long-term memory, resulting in improved performance. The new architecture allows for efficient handling of iterative data analysis and hypothesis refinement. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
